title: For One Bowl of Stew — Gathered to His People, Twins, Contempt
blocks: Peace be with you, brothers and sisters. Our last lesson ended in an evening: Isaac out in the field, meditating; he lifted up his eyes, and there were the camels coming. Today's chapter has one man to see off, and two children to welcome in.
And the question this lesson puts to us is about something every one of us has done: have you ever, when you were very hungry and very tired, made a decision you went on to regret?

Working late into the night, you buy something you don't need without thinking twice. Straight after a row, you fire off a message on impulse. Under the last ounce of pressure, you say one sentence you can never take back.
When a person is worn out, his judgement collapses altogether, and one sentence is all that is left inside him: I want it now.

Let me put the answer up front. The point is not that Esau sold. The point is that he did not care. Sell what is for ever to buy what is for now, and the bill takes a lifetime to pay — and some doors, once they close, do not open again.

Verses 7 and 8: "These are the days of the years of Abraham's life which he lived: one hundred seventy-five years. Abraham gave up his spirit, and died at a good old age, an old man, and full of years, and was gathered to his people."
Brothers and sisters, read those few words slowly.

"At a good old age, an old man" — in Hebrew בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה זָקֵן (*besevah tovah zaqen*), "in a good grey head, old." And back in 15:15 God had promised him, "but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age." That is the very same Hebrew phrase, בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה, word for word — a sentence spoken sixty years earlier, and it came true down to the syllable.
And the word that follows "an old man" is וְשָׂבֵעַ (*vesavea*), which literally means "full, having eaten his fill." This life of his had been enough.

Brothers and sisters, this is worth turning over slowly. By the time he died, had he received the land God promised him? No — all he owned was a cave. Had he seen his offspring as the stars of the sky? No — he saw one son and a handful of grandsons, and beyond that nothing had yet been born.
And Hebrews 11:13 says of people like him, "These all died in faith, not having received the promises."
And the epitaph Scripture gives him is this one word: full.
You can die with promises still unredeemed in your hands, and still be called satisfied. Brothers and sisters, that is what this chapter has to say to every older person sitting in the room.

"And was gathered to his people" — in Hebrew וַיֵּאָסֶף אֶל־עַמָּיו (*vayye'asef el-ammav*), literally "and he was gathered in to his own kin." Notice that the verb is passive: somebody came to collect him. And Abraham's own fathers were buried in Ur and in Haran, while he was buried at Machpelah — so this sentence cannot possibly mean no more than being laid in the family grave. The Old Testament speaks about the life to come with great reserve, but it never once treats a dead person as simply finished. And in Matthew 22:32 the Lord Jesus says, "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." He was reading the resurrection straight out of the names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
And verse 9 holds one more detail, a very beautiful one: "Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah."

Brothers and sisters, those two brothers were torn apart once — one driven out, one kept at home — and now, decades later, they are standing side by side at their father's grave. The text does not report a single word that passed between them. Some fractures take many years to heal, and the place where the healing happens is very often a funeral.
"Abraham gave up his spirit, and died at a good old age, an old man, and full of years" — what does it mean to be full of years?

The Hebrew שָׂבֵעַ (*sava*) is the word for being full after a meal. So this is not "he lived long enough"; it is "he lived full enough." And what deserves attention is that he never did receive what was promised: he did not get the land, he only bought a cave; he saw one son, he never saw the many nations. And yet the text calls him full. There is a deep reminder in that for us: being full is not the same as having arrived. Being full is knowing that the road you walked was the right road. In practice you can put one question to yourself — if my journey ended today, is the unsettled feeling in me there because I did not get what I wanted, or because I went in the wrong direction? Those are two different kinds of unsettledness, and they have to be handled separately.
Isaac and Ishmael buried their father together. Why is that one sentence worth noticing?

Verse 9: "Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah." The last time these two men appeared in the same frame, one was being driven out and one was staying at home. The text does not explain what happened in between; it simply sets them side by side in front of their father's grave. That is the restraint you meet again and again in Scripture — it lets the fact speak for itself. And the picture is precious: some relationships never fully recover while both parties are alive, and yet on one particular occasion the two of them stand together again. So do not treat "we have not been reconciled" as a verdict fixed for ever. And do not, out of a longing for a tidy ending, force a relationship that is not ready yet.
2. Two Nations Are in Your Womb
Verse 21: "Isaac entreated Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived."

Brothers and sisters, notice a detail that is very easy to read straight past: verse 20 says Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to be his wife, and verse 26 says he was sixty years old when she bore the twins.

The pattern in this family is unmistakable. Sarah waited twenty-five years. Rebekah waited twenty. Later on Rachel would wait a long time too. Over and over in this household God does the same thing in the same way — he brings the child of the promise out of a situation where nobody could wait any longer.
Verse 22: "The children struggled together within her. She said, 'If it is like this, why do I live?' She went to inquire of Yahweh."
And verse 23, God's answer: "Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger."

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the key quotation of Romans chapter 9. Paul writes there, "For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad … it was said to her, 'The elder will serve the younger.'"

And here I want to lay the readings out carefully. Some read this as plain proof of God's sovereign election of individuals. Others point out that the text itself says, "Two nations are in your womb" — so what it speaks of first is a matter between one people and another, and Edom did in fact come to serve Israel later on (2 Samuel 8:14). Others again argue that God foresaw Esau's character, though Paul says explicitly that this word came before either child had "done anything good or bad."

The position of these notes is this: what the verse speaks of first is which of the two carries the line forward, not a sentence passed on the eternal destiny of two men; and the principle of election that Paul sees in it does genuinely stand.

And let me add a pastoral word. Predestination is the doctrine most likely to start a quarrel in a church. What both sides agree on is this — nobody ever climbed up to God under his own power. Hold on to that, and the rest can be talked through slowly. And notice that when Paul finishes Romans 9 to 11 he does not draw a conclusion. He starts singing: "Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God!"
"Two nations are in your womb" — God chose Jacob before the twins were even born. Is that fair?

This is precisely the question Paul takes head on in Romans 9, and this is the verse he quotes. Down the centuries there have been two great readings. The first: election is God's sovereign predetermination, and human behaviour is not its cause. The second: God's foreknowledge and the human response stand together. Godly interpreters are found on both sides, and these notes will not settle the matter from the pulpit. What is certain is where Scripture itself puts the weight: this election is not a privilege handed to Jacob, it is a responsibility laid on him — "The elder will serve the younger" — and that line runs at last to the Messiah. And remember this as well: the man who was chosen then spent the next twenty years living in a thoroughly wretched way. Being chosen is not the same as having an easy road.
Rebekah "went to inquire of Yahweh." How exactly did she inquire?

The text does not tell us the method. It only says that she went, and that God answered. And that in itself is worth learning: her first move was not to find someone to consult, and not to work out an explanation of her own — it was to go and ask God. And the question she asked was very honest: "If it is like this, why do I live?" That is what a woman says when the pregnancy hurts so much that she does not want to be alive, and Scripture writes it down exactly as it stands. There are two things in this for us. First, the first step in a hard place is to inquire, not to explain. Second, you are allowed to say the ugliest sentence in you straight to God. And what she received after she had asked was not pain relief. It was a bigger picture — she now knew that the two children in her womb were two nations.
3. A Light from the Original: Four Verbs
Verse 27: "The boys grew. Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob was a quiet man, living in tents."
And verse 28 is the crack running right through this household: "Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob."
Brothers and sisters, look how blunt the reason is that the text gives for Isaac: "because he ate his venison." And on Rebekah's side, the text does not trouble to give a reason at all.
This family had already begun taking sides in the parents' generation. And the deception in chapter 27 has its root right here, in this one verse.
Verses 29 to 34 are that bowl of red stew.

Esau comes in from the field, "famished." He says, "Please feed me with some of that red stew, for I am famished." What he actually says in Hebrew is a good deal coarser than that: הַלְעִיטֵנִי נָא מִן־הָאָדֹם הָאָדֹם הַזֶּה — "let me gulp down some of that red stuff, that red stuff." He cannot even be bothered to ask what the soup is called.
Jacob says, "First, sell me your birthright."
Esau says, "Behold, I am about to die. What good is the birthright to me?"

Brothers and sisters, he is not about to die. A hunter does not die from missing one meal. But in that moment he genuinely felt that he was dying. And that is the most frightening thing about exhaustion — it turns "right now" into "everything."
And then comes verse 34, where the text uses four verbs, one after another, moving as fast as a man in a hurry:
"He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way."
Ate, drank, rose, went. Four actions, not one line of dialogue, not a flicker of hesitation, not one backward glance.
And then the author delivers the one comment he makes in the whole chapter: "So Esau despised his birthright."
"Despised" is בָּזָה (*bazah*) — to hold in contempt, to treat as worth nothing.

Brothers and sisters, the point is not that he sold. The point is that he did not care. The text does not say he was sorry afterwards. It does not say he beat his breast. He finished eating and walked away.
"So Esau despised his birthright" — where does the weight of that comment fall?

Verse 34 gives us four verbs in a row — "He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way" — and only then does the text pass judgement: "So Esau despised his birthright." Hebrew narrative very rarely comments directly, and when it does comment, that is the point. And "despised" (בָּזָה) is a strong word; it means to reckon a thing not worth mentioning. So the problem is not that he was hungry. The problem is the price his heart had already put on that birthright. Hebrews 12:16 calls him a "profane person … who sold his birthright for one meal," and goes on to say that afterwards "he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears." Some things, once sold, cannot be bought back with tears.
So what was it that he actually sold?

In an ordinary household the birthright carried two things: the double portion of the estate laid down in Deuteronomy 21:17, and the duty, once the father had died, of leading the whole family and presiding over its sacrifices.
But in this household the birthright meant something else again: taking up the promise that "all the families of the earth will be blessed through you."
Brothers and sisters, what he sold was not a share of the family estate. It was that promise.

And Hebrews 12:16 and 17 put the matter very heavily: "lest there be any sexually immoral person or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal. For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears."
"Though he sought it diligently with tears" — so he did weep, later on. Genesis 27:34 says that he "cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry."

Brothers and sisters, this is the heaviest thing in the chapter: some doors, once they are shut, do not open again. That is not said in order to frighten anybody. It is said so that today you will treasure the one that is still open.

And every act of contempt has the same structure: what is in front of you is concrete, and what is far off is abstract. That bowl of stew was hot, it smelled good, you could see it. That promise lay several hundred years away and could not be seen at all.
So which decision of yours this week is trading away the abstract to get the concrete?
What was the birthright, exactly, and why did it matter so much?

It had three layers: the double portion of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17); the spiritual and administrative leadership of the family; and — the weightiest of all in this particular household — the place that carries the covenant made with Abraham. Which is to say, it was not merely property. It was the line along which "all the families of the earth will be blessed." So what Esau sold was not the price of a meal; it was a trust handed down through the generations. And this is very practical for us. The things most easily sold off cheap today are exactly the things that carry no visible price — time, a good name, the relationships at home, closeness to God. There is no price tag on them, so a person feels nothing at the moment of selling.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching Esau as a man who was born bad. What Hebrews rebukes in him is that he was "profane" and that he "despised" — that is his attitude in the moment, not a verdict fixed on him from birth. Preach it as fate and your congregation learns nothing about the choice made in that moment, and they walk out thinking, "Well, it was all settled anyway."

The second is preaching Jacob's exploitation of a man at his weakest as spiritual insight. Some who teach this passage will say, "Jacob had real spiritual discernment; he knew how to value a birthright." But look carefully: he named his price only after he had seen his brother collapsing with hunger. And God had already announced in verse 23 that the elder would serve the younger — the thing was his already, and he chose to get it by a transaction. That Scripture's closing comment falls on Esau does not make Jacob right; Jacob's bill is the twenty years of running that come next.

The third is using the doctrine of election to make people stop preaching the gospel. Romans teaches election in order to comfort those who already believe, not to make anyone give up inviting. The same Paul says in Romans 10, "How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?"

The fourth is preaching the consequences and never preaching the door that is still open. In chapter 33 Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and the two of them weep; in chapter 36 God gives him Mount Seir, and he becomes the father of a nation. If all you preach is what he lost, then everyone in the room who has ever sold something important will finish the sermon stuck in despair.

The fifth is making a great deal out of the passage where Abraham marries Keturah. The text passes no comment on that marriage; it settles one thing only. Verse 5 says, "Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac," and the other sons were given gifts and then sent away eastward. The line of the covenant was not diluted. What the author cares about is the outcome of the inheritance, not an assessment of the marriage.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the most painful thing in a Chinese family is dividing the estate, and it usually detonates only after the parents have died. What does this chapter have to say about that? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives three very practical reminders. First, settle the boundaries while you are still alive. Verses 5 and 6 say that Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac, gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, and sent them away. He divided it up while he was still living; he left no fog behind for the children to guess at. Second, favouritism sends in its bill. That line in verse 28 — "Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison" — looks like nothing more than a family quirk, and by chapter 27 it has exploded. Third, and most important of all: what is the real birthright? In this household it was not the double portion of property, it was the promise. And in our households, what are we leaving our children — the house, or the faith? Brothers and sisters, how many Chinese families divide the property down to the last detail and never hand on the faith? The house gets divided in the end, and the brothers and sisters are scattered along with it.

The second question: once, in a moment when I was exhausted and acting on impulse, I made a decision that I am still paying for today. Is there still a chance for me? Brothers and sisters, let me answer honestly, in two halves. The first half is this: some consequences genuinely cannot be recalled. Hebrews says of Esau that "he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears" — Scripture does not pretend that everything can be done over. The other half is this: a consequence that cannot be recalled does not mean that God has given up on you. Look at where Esau ends up. In chapter 33 he runs to embrace the very brother who cheated him; in chapter 36 God gives him the whole of Mount Seir. He lost the birthright; he did not lose the mercy of God. So the sentence I want to put into your hands is this: stop spending your strength trying to reopen the door that is already shut, and put your strength into the one that is still open. God still has work to do in the years you have left.
How do I know when I am selling something important off cheap?

Three indicators, and all three are useful. First, does it have a price? The things with no price tag are the easiest to trade away — that one hour with your child, for instance. Second, am I exhausted or in a hurry at the moment of the transaction? Esau sold when he was "famished"; a person running on empty will see the one bowl of stew in front of him as bigger than a lifelong birthright. Third, do I avoid the subject afterwards? People who know in their hearts that they sold at a loss usually do not want to talk about it. If two of the three are true, stop there, write the matter down and find someone to talk to. And the best prevention of all is this: set your boundaries in advance, while you are not tired.
7. Living 321 Out — Do Not Let the Feeling of the Moment Set the Price
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Esau went hungry for a day and traded what is for ever for what is for now. And in Matthew chapter 4 the Lord Jesus fasted forty days and forty nights in the wilderness, and afterwards he was hungry, and the devil said, "If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread." He answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God's mouth.'" Brothers and sisters, the same hunger, and two different answers. My role model is this: at his hungriest, he still would not trade the long view away for the thing in front of him.

The Bible is my standard — and the standard this chapter gives is one very simple question: is this thing for ever, or is it only for now? Brothers and sisters, you do not have to work the sums out finely every time. You only have to ask that one question before you press the button on a decision. Most regret comes out of the one second in which nobody asked.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice the state Esau was in. When a person is worn out he is least able to hear guidance, and most likely to mistake an impulse for a need. When Elijah lay under the broom tree asking to die, the first thing God did was to let him eat and let him sleep (1 Kings 19). So looking after your own body is part of spiritual warfare. It is not a fleshly concern.

Let Jesus be King — that line in verse 23, "The elder will serve the younger," was spoken by God before either child had been born. Which is to say, my worth is fixed somewhere outside me. Letting Jesus be King means handing him even the question of what I am worth, and letting him be the one who says. Brothers and sisters, this dismantles a great deal of anxiety — you do not have to use achievement to prove that you are worth something.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — neither brother in this chapter comes out of it looking respectable: one of them despises, the other loots a burning house. And God's plan goes on regardless. The glory does not rest on either of them. It rests on the God who does not alter his plan because of what human beings got up to.

Establish God's system — in verse 9, two brothers who had once been torn apart bury their father together. Brothers and sisters, some fractures take many years to heal. And to establish God's system is to make the boundaries and the inheritance plain while you are still alive — do not leave a fog behind you, so that the children only begin to quarrel in front of your grave.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We are fond of saying that if you change the mindset you change the life — and Esau is an excellent example running the other way. His problem was not that he did not know a birthright was valuable. He knew. In chapter 27 he is in tears trying to fight it back. His problem was that in those thirty exhausted seconds, his mindset never turned into action. So the renewing of the mindset has to be paired with something that sounds thoroughly unspiritual — rest properly, eat properly, keep away from the hour that reduces your judgement to zero. A servant of God who is chronically short of sleep and running on an empty tank is the one most likely to sell something at the door.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Bowl of Stew
Brothers and sisters, one and the same bowl of red stew falls into four kinds of heart, and what each of them sees is different.

The proud heart says, "Esau had no sense of value at all." This heart finishes the chapter quite certain that it would never be that stupid. Brothers and sisters, think it over: Esau genuinely believed that he was about to die. And a person in the last stages of exhaustion never feels that he is doing something foolish — he only feels that he is solving an urgent problem. That decision you made late at night, the last time: it felt perfectly reasonable then too.

The fearful heart says, "Have I already sold something?" This heart finishes the chapter and starts turning over its own past. To a heart like that I want to say: the point of this chapter is not to audit yesterday, it is to protect tomorrow. Rather than going back to count, write down now one thing you have resolved never to sell.

The ashamed heart says, "I am the one who sold." It may well be true that at some moment you traded the long view for the thing in front of you — a marriage, a child's childhood, your integrity. Brothers and sisters, look at what Esau turns into later on: in chapter 33 he runs to his brother, embraces him, kisses him, and the two of them weep. Scripture does not write a single word about the work God did in him, but that embrace was real. God did not give up on the man who had sold his birthright.

The wounded heart says, "I am the one whose burning house was looted." It may be that at your weakest someone close to you took advantage of you — you signed a paper you should never have signed, you agreed to something you should never have agreed to. Brothers and sisters, notice the attitude of the text: it does pass judgement on Esau, but it also records in full exactly how Jacob named his price, and then it settles Jacob's account with twenty years of running. God saw what was done, and he keeps the books more accurately than we do.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, identify your own "hour of exhaustion." Everyone has a stretch of the day when judgement drops to zero — late at night, after overtime, straight after a row, when the blood sugar has crashed. Write it down, and then make yourself one rule: in that stretch, no decisions, no replies to messages, nothing ordered.

Second, write down one thing you have resolved never to sell. Just one. It might be the Lord's Day; it might be your integrity; it might be the twenty minutes you give your child every day. Write it down and stick it up where you will see it.
Third, get one proper night's sleep. This is not a joke. Under the broom tree, the first things God gave Elijah were bread and sleep. On at least one day this week, go to bed an hour earlier.

Fourth, make one foggy thing plain. Is there something at home that everybody is guessing at and nobody dares to raise — the inheritance, who takes which share of caring for your parents, some promise that was made? Abraham divided it up while he was still alive. Open your mouth once this week.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible who came home from hunting worn out and traded his birthright for a bowl of red stew; and the comment Scripture makes is not "what a fool" but "he despised it" — the point is not that he sold, it is that he did not care; so here is the thing I learned, that a person's most dangerous moment is not the moment of temptation, it is the moment when he is so tired that nothing is left in him but "I want it now."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer let the feeling of the moment set the price, and sell what is for ever for one bowl of stew.
I declare that in the hour of exhaustion I will stop, and I will not make my decisions then.
I declare that my worth is fixed in God, and that I do not have to prove it with achievement.
I declare that while I am still alive I will say plainly the things that need to be said plainly.
I am supposed to "hold on to one thing that has no price tag" this week — but I am tired every single day. How am I meant to hold on to anything?

It is precisely because you are tired that the thing has to be settled in advance. Three ways to do it. First, put it in your diary, so that it becomes an appointment with a time on it rather than something you will get to when you have a spare moment. Second, set a minimum: not "an hour with my child every day" but "ten minutes a day, with the phone put away" — small enough that you could still do it on your most exhausted day. Third, find someone to ask you about it: one person's willpower gets eaten alive by fatigue, but one question from somebody else works remarkably well. And let me say one more thing honestly: if you are so tired for so long that you cannot hold on to anything at all, then what needs dealing with may not be your discipline but your hours and your load, and that has to be faced as well.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, let it be the four verbs strung together in verse 34:
"He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way."
No pause, no backward look, not one word. He finished eating, he got up, he went.
And afterwards the author adds one more sentence: "So Esau despised his birthright."
Brothers and sisters, picture that scene: a man sells, in thirty seconds, something that carries several hundred years inside it, and then dusts off his hands and walks away without feeling a thing.
The most frightening part is not the transaction. It is that "went his way."

And at the top of the very same chapter, another man's departure is written like this: "Abraham gave up his spirit, and died at a good old age, an old man, and full of years, and was gathered to his people." He had nothing in his hands — one cave, one son, a heap of promises not yet redeemed. And Scripture says that he was full.
Brothers and sisters, two departures in one chapter. One man received nothing and was full; the other man ate his fill and lost everything.

And in Matthew 16:26 the Lord Jesus asks a question that reads exactly like a footnote to this chapter: "For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life?"

The focus is not on how much I gained in this life, not on what I once sold, and not on whether that door is still open. The focus is on Jesus — at his hungriest he still would not trade what is for ever for what is for now, and then he laid down his life for us as well. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to recognise our own hour of exhaustion, and to write down one thing we have resolved never to sell. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the ordinary days. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ The original behind "full of years" is "having eaten his fill." Why would a man who never received the promise be full?
2. ★★★ "Despised" is a heavy word. What was it that Esau actually sold? And what is most easily sold off cheap today?
3. ★ Rebekah was in such distress that she said, "Why do I live?" — and yet her first move was to go and inquire of Yahweh. What does that order of hers remind you of?
4. ★★ Being chosen is not the same as having an easy road — Jacob, the chosen one, spent the next twenty years living wretchedly. How should that correct our picture of what it is to be chosen?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone speaks in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I would never sell anything for a bowl of stew), fearful (I am afraid I will not get through what is in front of me), ashamed (I have sold something that really mattered), wounded (somebody once traded on my weakness for their own gain). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "So Esau despised his birthright." Then tell the group — where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Think back over the last six months. What is one decision you made when you were at your most exhausted? Looking back now, was the price on that decision reckoned rightly?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing in my life that carries no price tag and yet matters most is …"
9. ★★ This week, what minimum will you set for that one thing — small enough that you could still do it on your most exhausted day? Say it out loud.

Leader's reminder: question nine may touch regret and self-blame. Do not let group members review one another's decisions, and do not say "if only you had known." If anyone speaks of long-term exhaustion, care for him privately after the meeting and help him deal with his hours and his load.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ At home, which stretch of your time is most easily eaten up by other things? How will you put it into your diary this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, at what moment are you most likely to agree to something you should not agree to?
12. ★★★ The practice of not deciding while exhausted: this week, every important decision waits a night before you answer. Say how you are going to remind yourself.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the minimum you have set, and ask him to check on you every second day. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who went hungry for one meal and sold his birthright. Second: the comment Scripture makes on him is three words — he despised it. Third: so I have started paying attention to what I trade away when I am at my most tired. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one thing you will hold on to this week, and the minimum you have set. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us from selling off cheap, in our exhaustion, the portion that he has given us.
